Ionisation of a solid metal atom

questions.question:
Calculate the standard cell potential (in V) of the cell in which the following reaction takes place:

{Fe}^{2 + }\left(aq\right) + A{g}^{ + }\left(aq\right) \to F{e}^{3 + }\left(aq\right) + Ag(s)$

Given that

{E}_{{\mathrm{Ag}}^{ + } / Ag}^{o} = xV {E}_{{Fe}^{2 + } / Fe}^{o} = yV {E}_{{Fe}^{3 + } / Fe}^{o} = zV$
questions.explanation:
$\overset{A}{F{e}^{ + 2}} + \overset{C}{A{g}^{ + }} \to F{e}^{3 + } + Ag {E}_{cell}^{o} = SRP$ of cathode $- SRP$ of anode

$= {E}_{A{g}^{ + } | Ag}^{o} - {E}_{F{e}^{ + 3} | F{e}^{ + 2}}^{o} = x - {E}_{F{e}^{3 + } | F{e}^{ + 2}}^{o}$

Since $E ^\circ$ cell is an intensive property, the $E ^\circ$ cell values are not additive by nature. But the standard Gibbs free energy change is an extensive property and hence can be added.

(i) $F{e}^{ + 3} \to Fe + 3{e}^{ - } \to Z = {E}_{1}^{o};\text{ }\Delta {G}_{1} = - 3 \times F \times z$

(ii) $F{e}^{ + 2} \to Fe + 2{e}^{ - } Y = {E}_{2}^{o}; \Delta {G}_{2} = - 2 \times F \times y$

Subtracting (ii) from (i)

$F{e}^{ + 3} \to F{e}^{ + 2} \Delta {G}_{3} = \Delta {G}_{1} - \Delta {G}_{2} \left({E}^{o} = - 2y + 3z\right) {E}_{cell}^{o} = x - \left( - 2y + 3z\right) = x + 2y - 3z$

questions.explanation:
The given cell reaction is:

$\dfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_{2(g)} + \text{AgCl}_{(s)} \rightarrow \text{H}^{+}_{(aq)} + \text{Cl}^{-}_{(aq)} + \text{Ag}_{(s)}$

The reaction can be split into two half-reactions.

Oxidation half-reaction (at anode):

$\dfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}^{+}_{(aq)} + e^{-}$

Reduction half-reaction (at cathode):

$\text{AgCl}_{(s)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}_{(s)} + \text{Cl}^{-}_{(aq)}$

The anode consists of hydrogen gas being oxidized to $\text{H}^{+}$ ions on a platinum electrode. This half-cell is represented as $\text{Pt} | \text{H}_{2(g)} | \text{H}^{+}_{(aq)}$.

The cathode involves the reduction of solid $\text{AgCl}$ to solid $\text{Ag}$, releasing $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions into the solution. This is a metal-insoluble salt electrode, represented as $\text{Cl}^{-}_{(aq)} | \text{AgCl}_{(s)} | \text{Ag}$.

Combining the two half-cells, we need an electrolyte that contains both $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions. An aqueous solution of $\text{HCl}$ serves this purpose perfectly as a common electrolyte without the need for a salt bridge.

The complete galvanic cell is represented by writing the anode on the left and the cathode on the right, separated by the common electrolyte:

$\text{Pt} | \text{H}_{2(g)} | \text{HCl}_{(\text{soln.})} | \text{AgCl}_{(s)} | \text{Ag}$

questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & 2 \mathrm{e}^{-}+2 \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \\ & \mathrm{E}=\mathrm{E}^{\circ}-\frac{0.059}{\mathrm{n}} \log \frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]^2} \\ & 0=0-\frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{\left(10^{-7}\right)^2} \\ & \log \frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{\left(10^{-7}\right)^2}=0 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{10^{-14}}=1 \\ & \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{H}_2}=10^{-14} \text { bar }\end{aligned}$

(B) an aqueous solution of $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ using platinum electrodes. (C) a dilute solution of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$ using platinum electrodes. (D) a high concentration solution of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$ using platinum electrodes.
